'''Karen L. Kavanagh''' is a professor of [[physics]] at [[Simon Fraser University]] in [[Burnaby]], British Columbia, Canada, where she heads the Kavanagh Lab, a research lab working on [[semiconductor]] [[nanoscience]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.sfu.ca/kavanaghlab.html |title=Kavanagh Lab |publisher=Simon Fraser University |accessdate=9 November 2012}}</ref>

==Education==
Kavanagh obtained a BSc in Chemical-Physics from [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in 1978, followed by 3 years at [[Bell Northern Research]] in Ottawa in their Advanced Technology Laboratory. She received her PhD in materials science and engineering in 1987 at [[Cornell University]] in [[Ithaca, New York]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Karen Kavanagh, Professor |url=http://www.physics.sfu.ca/people/profiles/kavanagh |work=Department of Physics |publisher=Simon Fraser University |accessdate=9 November 2012 |archive-date=1 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131201013131/http://www.physics.sfu.ca/people/profiles/kavanagh |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
After post doctoral work at [[IBM]] and [[MIT]], Kavanagh accepted a faculty position in the Electrical and Computer Engineering Dept. at the [[University of California, San Diego]]. She has been at Simon Fraser University since 2000.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physics - Karen L. Kavanagh |url=https://physics.aps.org/authors/karen_l_kavanagh |access-date=2025-06-11 |website=physics.aps.org |language=en}}</ref>

Her main field of interest is electronic [[materials science]] – studying the effects of defects on the properties of [[semiconductor material]]s and devices. She has worked on strain relaxation in lattice-mismatched semiconductor [[heterostructure]]s, [[diffusion barrier]]s and electrical contacts for silicon and [[III-V semiconductor]] based devices, [[epitaxial]] growth and [[nucleation]], and [[electron transport]] through [[thin film]]s and interfaces. Her work on [[Characterization (materials science)|characterization]] tools including [[electron microscopy]], [[Rutherford backscattering]], [[x-ray diffraction]], and [[scanning probe microscopy]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Our Group |url=https://www.sfu.ca/kavanaghlab/about-our-group.html |access-date=2025-06-11 |website=www.sfu.ca}}</ref>

She is a Fellow of the [[Institute of Physics]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Karen L. Kavanagh |url=http://physics.aps.org/authors/karen_l_kavanagh |work=Physics |publisher=American Physical Society |accessdate=9 November 2012}}</ref> and is the author of over 200 journal papers and conference proceedings, as shown on [[ORCID]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=ORCID|title=Karen L. Kavanagh (0000-0002-3059-7528)|url=https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3059-7528|access-date=2021-02-09|website=orcid.org|language=en}}</ref> In 2022, Kavanagh was selected as a Fellow of the [[Materials Research Society]] (MRS). <ref>{{Cite web |title=List of MRS Fellows |url=https://www.mrs.org/advancing-careers/award-central/spring-awards/mrs-fellows/list-of-mrs-fellows |access-date=2025-06-11 |website=www.mrs.org |language=en}}</ref>

*NSERC University Faculty Awardee (1999)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sfu.ca/archive-sfunews/sfnews/1999/May20/femalerep.html|title=SF News – May 20, 1999 – 100 per cent success rate in NSERC awards|publisher=Simon Fraser University|access-date=2018-03-24}}</ref>
*NSF [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]] (1991)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://grantome.com/grant/NSF/DMR-9157724|title=Presidential Young Investigator Award: Kavanagh, Karen|publisher=Grantome|accessdate=5 November 2014 |last1=Kavanagh |first1=Karen }}</ref>
